intro: Hi class — I'm Dr. Marcus Vela. I help design wind turbines, and the thing I love most is that a turbine is honest: it records everything it does, minute by minute. Today we'll watch one real turbine work for half a day. Then I want every group to tell me what you noticed about the shape it drew. There are no wrong answers — just different angles.
act1Post: Every dot you just saw is one real minute of one turbine's life — the wind speed it felt, and the power it made. Two numbers each. Put them all on the same plane and the turbine draws a curve. Don't name the shape yet. Tell me what you see — every group.
act2Picker: Now you investigate. Different tools test different ideas. Fitting a curve asks 'what equation matches?' Differences ask 'is it really a parabola?' Splitting it into zones asks 'where does the model actually hold?' There's no right tool — pick what fits the wonderings up there, and write down what each one shows.
act3Top: No answer was wrong. Every group's notice and wonder was a real piece of the picture — even the ones that contradicted each other. Below, you'll see what every group found, side by side. Then I'll show you the math that ties it together.
act3Closing: Thanks for modeling with me. A parabola fits the rising part of this curve beautifully — but the real physics is a little wilder, and that flat top was a design choice, built in on purpose. The next time you drive past a wind farm, you'll know exactly what those blades are doing, and why every model has limits.
howItWorksWind: Let's start from the beginning. The wind carries kinetic energy — moving air, ready to do work. The blades are shaped like airplane wings, and when wind flows over them, it creates lift — the same force that lifts a plane off the runway. Except here, instead of lifting up, that pull yanks the blades around in a circle. That spin is the rotor. It's slow but powerful — about 15 revolutions per minute, with enough torque to turn the whole machine.
howItWorksNacelle: Now inside the nacelle. That slow spin enters through the low-speed shaft. The gearbox uses interlocking gears — a large gear turning a small one — to multiply the spin from roughly 20 RPM to over 1200 RPM. That high-speed spin feeds the generator, where magnets and copper coils convert motion into electricity. This is where the actual power is made.
howItWorksGrid: The electricity travels down a power cable inside the tower to a transformer at the base, which steps up the voltage for long-distance transmission. From there it joins the grid — the same grid that powers lights, computers, and factories. Every single dot you are about to see in the data was measured right inside this generator, minute by minute.
howItWorksBridge: So when we talk about the power curve, we're talking about real physics happening in real time. Wind speed is measured by an anemometer on the nacelle. Power output is measured by sensors on the generator. The shape that data draws is the signature of everything we just walked through.
synthesize: Step back. Across every lens, what pulls it together? Pick the statements your class is ready to defend — that's the claim you carry into the reveal.
